questions.question: Suppose a program is running on a non-pipelined single processor computer system. The computer is connected to an external device that can interrupt the processor asynchronously. The processor needs to execute the interrupt service routine (ISR) to serve this interrupt. The following steps (not necessarily in order) are taken by the processor when the interrupt arrives: (i) The processor saves the content of the program counter. (ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR. (iii) The processor finishes the present instruction. Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT sequence of steps?
questions.explanation: On an asynchronous interrupt, the processor must first reach a clean state before it can safely switch control: 1. (iii) The processor finishes the present instruction — interrupts are only serviced at instruction boundaries, never mid-instruction. 2. (i) The processor saves the content of the program counter — so execution can later resume exactly where it left off. 3. (ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR — only now does control actually transfer to the ISR. Answer: (iii), (i), (ii) Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Which ONE of the following techniques used in compiler code optimization uses live variable analysis?
questions.explanation: Live variable analysis determines, at each point in the program, which variables' current values might still be used later (i.e. are "live"). This information is exactly what's needed to decide which variables are worth keeping in fast registers versus which can be safely evicted — that's the core of register allocation/assignment . Run-time function call management, strength reduction, and constant folding are all real optimizations, but none of them fundamentally depend on liveness information the way register allocation does. Answer: Register assignment to variables Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Consider the following [latex]B^+[/latex] tree with 5 nodes, in which a node can store at most 3 key values. The value 23 is now inserted in the [latex]B^+[/latex] tree. Which of the following options(s) is/are CORRECT?

options.A: None of the nodes will split.
options.B: At least one node will split and redistribute.
options.C: The total number of nodes will remain same.
options.D: The height of the tree will increase.

questions.explanation: Inserting a new key into a [latex]B^+[/latex] tree always follows the same pattern: search down to the correct leaf, insert the key there in sorted order, and if that leaf now holds more than the maximum allowed keys (here, more than [latex]3[/latex]), it must split into two leaves , pushing/copying up a separator key into the parent. Since the target leaf here is already at its maximum capacity of [latex]3[/latex] keys before inserting [latex]23[/latex], it overflows and must split; this new separator key then gets inserted into the parent node, which can itself overflow and split further, potentially propagating all the way up to a new root. Whenever a split reaches (or creates a new) root, the height of the tree increases by one level . Splitting always increases the total node count (a leaf becomes two, or an internal node splits into two) — it never leaves the count unchanged, and "no node splits" is only possible if the target leaf had spare capacity, which it did not here. Answer: At least one node will split and redistribute; and the height of the tree will increase. Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Consider the 3-way handshaking protocol for TCP connection establishment. Let the three packets exchanged during the connection establishment be denoted as P1, P2, and P3, in order. Which of the following option(s) is/are TRUE with respect to TCP header flags that are set in the packets?

So the correct flags are P1: SYN=1, and P2: SYN=1 & ACK=1. Answer: P2 (SYN=1, ACK=1), and P1 (SYN=1) Click here for detail solution

options.A: There is exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] for which the above system of equations has no solution.
options.B: There exist an infinite number of values of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has no solution.
options.C: There exists exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has exactly one solution.
options.D: There exists exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has an infinite number of solutions.

questions.explanation: [latex]\begin{cases}x+ky=1\\kx+y=-1\end{cases}[/latex], with determinant [latex]\Delta=1-k^2[/latex]. No solution requires [latex]\Delta=0[/latex] (i.e. [latex]k=\pm1[/latex]) and the two equations to actually be inconsistent (parallel but not identical lines): - [latex]k=1[/latex]: equations become [latex]x+y=1[/latex] and [latex]x+y=-1[/latex] — parallel, contradictory → no solution . - [latex]k=-1[/latex]: equations become [latex]x-y=1[/latex] and [latex]-x+y=-1[/latex], which is just the first equation multiplied by [latex]-1[/latex] — the same line → infinitely many solutions , not "no solution." So there is exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] (namely [latex]k=1[/latex]) giving no solution, and exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] (namely [latex]k=-1[/latex]) giving infinitely many solutions. For every other [latex]k[/latex] (i.e. [latex]k\ne\pm1[/latex]), [latex]\Delta\ne0[/latex] and there's a unique solution — but that happens for infinitely many values of [latex]k[/latex], not just one, so the "exactly one k gives a unique solution" claim is false. Answer: Exactly one k gives no solution; and exactly one k gives infinitely many solutions. Click here for detail solution

No solution requires [latex]\Delta=0[/latex] (i.e. [latex]k=\pm1[/latex]) and the two equations to actually be inconsistent (parallel but not identical lines):
- [latex]k=1[/latex]: equations become [latex]x+y=1[/latex] and [latex]x+y=-1[/latex] — parallel, contradictory → no solution.
- [latex]k=-1[/latex]: equations become [latex]x-y=1[/latex] and [latex]-x+y=-1[/latex], which is just the first equation multiplied by [latex]-1[/latex] — the same line → infinitely many solutions, not "no solution."

So there is exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] (namely [latex]k=1[/latex]) giving no solution, and exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] (namely [latex]k=-1[/latex]) giving infinitely many solutions. For every other [latex]k[/latex] (i.e. [latex]k\ne\pm1[/latex]), [latex]\Delta\ne0[/latex] and there's a unique solution — but that happens for infinitely many values of [latex]k[/latex], not just one, so the "exactly one k gives a unique solution" claim is false.

Answer: Exactly one k gives no solution; and exactly one k gives infinitely many solutions.

questions.question: Let [latex]X[/latex] be a 3-variable Boolean function that produces output as '1' when at least two of the input variables are '1'. Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT, where [latex]a, b, c, d, e[/latex] are Boolean variables?

options.A: [latex]X(a, b, X(c, d, e)) = X(X(a, b, c), d, e)[/latex]
options.B: [latex]X(a, b, X(a, b, c)) = X(a, b, c)[/latex]
options.C: [latex]X(a, b, X(a, c, d)) = (X(a, b, a) \text{ AND } X(c, d, c))[/latex]
options.D: [latex]X(a, b, c) = X(a, X(a, b, c), X(a, c, c))[/latex]

A useful fact: whenever two of the three inputs to [latex]X[/latex] are the same variable [latex]v[/latex], the output is forced to equal [latex]v[/latex] regardless of the third input (e.g. [latex]X(v,v,\text{anything})=v[/latex]). If [latex]a\ne b[/latex], then (since one of [latex]a,b[/latex] is [latex]0[/latex] and the other [latex]1[/latex]) [latex]m=c[/latex], and [latex]X(a,b,m)=X(a,b,c)=m[/latex]. questions.question: The number [latex]-6[/latex] can be represented as 1010 in 4-bit 2's complement representation. Which of the following is/are CORRECT 2's complement representation(s) of [latex]-6[/latex]?
questions.explanation: Correctly extending a two's-complement number to more bits requires sign-extension : replicate the sign bit (here, the leading [latex]1[/latex], since [latex]-6[/latex] is negative) into all the new higher-order bit positions — you cannot just prepend arbitrary/zero bits. [latex]-6[/latex] in 4-bit: [latex]1010[/latex]. Correct 8-bit sign-extension: [latex]1111\,1010[/latex] (four [latex]1[/latex]'s prepended). The alternative [latex]1000\,1010[/latex] incorrectly prepends [latex]1000[/latex] instead of replicating the sign bit — wrong. Correct 16-bit sign-extension: [latex]1111\,1111\,1111\,1010[/latex] (twelve [latex]1[/latex]'s prepended). The alternative [latex]1000\,0000\,0000\,1010[/latex] is similarly wrong. Answer: 1111 1010 (8-bit) and 1111 1111 1111 1010 (16-bit) Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE for any binary search tree (BST) having [latex]n[/latex] distinct integers?

options.A: The maximum length of a path from the root node to any other node is [latex](n - 1)[/latex].
options.B: An inorder traversal will always produce a sorted sequence of elements.
options.C: Finding an element takes [latex]O(\log_2 n)[/latex] time in the worst case.
options.D: Every BST is also a Min-Heap.

questions.explanation: Checking each BST claim for [latex]n[/latex] distinct integers: - Maximum path length from root to any node is [latex]n-1[/latex]: true — in the worst case (a completely skewed/degenerate BST, essentially a linked list), all [latex]n[/latex] nodes form a single chain, giving a root-to-deepest-node path of [latex]n-1[/latex] edges, which is also the largest this can ever be since there are only [latex]n[/latex] nodes total. - Inorder traversal always produces sorted order: true — this is the defining property of a BST (left subtree [latex]<[/latex] node [latex]<[/latex] right subtree, recursively), and it holds regardless of the tree's shape. - Finding an element takes [latex]O(\log_2n)[/latex] time in the worst case: false — that bound only holds for a balanced BST. A skewed/degenerate BST (as noted above) can force search time all the way up to [latex]O(n)[/latex]. - Every BST is also a Min-Heap: false — a min-heap requires every parent to be smaller than both children, but a BST only orders left [latex]<[/latex] parent [latex]<[/latex] right; nothing stops a BST's left child from being smaller than its grandparent in ways that violate heap order. Answer: Max path length is n-1; and inorder traversal always gives sorted order. Click here for detail solution

questions.question: A regular language [latex]L[/latex] is accepted by a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with [latex]n[/latex] states. Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE?

options.A: [latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting NFA with < [latex]n[/latex] states.
options.B: [latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting DFA with < [latex]n[/latex] states.
options.C: There exists a DFA with [latex]\leq 2^n[/latex] states that accepts [latex]L[/latex].
options.D: Every DFA that accepts [latex]L[/latex] has [latex]> 2^n[/latex] states.

questions.explanation: For a regular language [latex]L[/latex] accepted by some [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA, recall two standard facts: (1) subset construction always produces an equivalent DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states, and (2) NFA/DFA state counts for a given language are not unique — smaller equivalent automata can certainly exist. - "[latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting NFA with [latex]< n[/latex] states": could well be true (this [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA might not be minimal), so calling it FALSE is incorrect — it's a true possibility, not a false statement. - "[latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting DFA with [latex]< n[/latex] states": also entirely possible depending on the language, so this is also true (not false). - "There exists a DFA with [latex]\le 2^n[/latex] states accepting [latex]L[/latex]": guaranteed true by subset construction — so this is also true, not false. - "Every DFA that accepts L has [latex]> 2^n[/latex] states" : this directly contradicts the subset-construction guarantee (a DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states always exists) — so this statement is definitely FALSE . Answer: "Every DFA that accepts L has more than [latex]2^n[/latex] states" is the FALSE statement. Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Which ONE of the following languages is accepted by a deterministic pushdown automaton?

options.C: Any language accepted by a non-deterministic pushdown automaton.

questions.explanation: A deterministic pushdown automaton (DPDA) accepts exactly the class of deterministic context-free languages (DCFLs) , which is a proper subset of all context-free languages — some CFLs (like certain languages requiring "guessing" where a string's midpoint is) are inherently non-deterministic and can never be accepted by any DPDA, only by a general (non-deterministic) PDA. Since every regular language can always be recognized by a DFA (which is trivially also a valid DPDA that simply never uses its stack), every regular language is guaranteed accepted by some DPDA. "Any context-free language," "any NPDA-accepted language" (these are the same, broader class, and DPDA is a strictly weaker/smaller class), and "any decidable language" (a vastly larger class, including languages that aren't even context-free) are all too broad to be guaranteed DPDA-acceptable. Answer: Any regular language. Click here for detail solution

Answer: Consistency and Isolation Click here for detail solution

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS) on an undirected simple graph [latex]G [/latex] is/are TRUE?

options.A: A DFS tree of [latex]G [/latex] is a Shortest Path tree of [latex]G [/latex].
options.B: Every non-tree edge of [latex]G [/latex] with respect to a DFS tree is a forward/back edge.

questions.explanation: Checking each BFS/DFS claim on an undirected simple graph: - "A DFS tree is a shortest path tree": false — DFS explores as deep as possible along one branch first and gives no shortest-path guarantee at all; only BFS guarantees that. - "Every non-tree edge w.r.t. a DFS tree is a forward/back edge" : true — in an undirected graph, DFS can never produce a cross edge; every non-tree edge necessarily connects an ancestor-descendant pair (classified as a back edge, viewable from either endpoint as forward/back). - "Non-tree BFS edge (u,v): distances differ by at most 1" : true — this is a standard BFS property, since BFS explores level-by-level and any edge can only connect vertices in the same level or adjacent levels. - "Both BFS and DFS can find connected components" : true — running either traversal repeatedly from every yet-unvisited vertex correctly partitions the graph into its connected components. questions.question: An array [latex]A [/latex] of length [latex]n [/latex] with distinct elements is said to be bitonic if there is an index [latex]1 \leq i \leq n [/latex] such that [latex]A[1..i] [/latex] is sorted in the non-decreasing order and [latex]A[i+1..n] [/latex] is sorted in the non-increasing order. Which ONE of the following represents the best possible asymptotic bound for the worst-case number of comparisons by an algorithm that searches for an element in a bitonic array [latex]A [/latex]?

At any index, comparing the current element to its neighbors tells you which "half" (increasing or decreasing) you're in, and binary search can be adapted to search each half: First locate the peak (maximum) element using a binary-search-style approach in [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex] (comparing an element to its neighbors to decide which direction has the larger values). Once the peak is found, the array splits into two ordinary sorted sequences (one increasing, one decreasing), and each can be searched with ordinary binary search, also [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex]. Combining these steps keeps the total worst-case comparisons at [latex]\Theta(\log n)[/latex], matching what you'd get for a single sorted array — no better bound like [latex]\Theta(1)[/latex] is achievable (you must still narrow down the location), and no worse bound like [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex] or [latex]\Theta(\log^2n)[/latex] is necessary. Answer: Θ(log n) Click here for detail solution

\forall f, g \in \mathcal{F}, \, f \preceq g \quad \text{if and only if} \quad \forall x \in \{1, \dots, n\}, f(x) \leq g(x), \text{ where } 0 \leq 1.

questions.explanation: [latex]f\preceq g[/latex] iff [latex]f(x)\le g(x)[/latex] for every [latex]x[/latex] — this is the standard pointwise "less than or equal to" ordering on binary functions. - Reflexive: [latex]f(x)\le f(x)[/latex] always. Antisymmetric: if [latex]f\preceq g[/latex] and [latex]g\preceq f[/latex], then [latex]f(x)=g(x)[/latex] for all [latex]x[/latex], so [latex]f=g[/latex]. Transitive: chains through in the obvious way. So [latex]\preceq[/latex] is a genuine partial order (not symmetric, and not an equivalence relation, since e.g. [latex]f\preceq g[/latex] doesn't imply [latex]g\preceq f[/latex] unless [latex]f=g[/latex]). - Lattice: for any two functions [latex]f,g[/latex], their pointwise max (taking [latex]\max(f(x),g(x))[/latex] at every [latex]x[/latex]) is their least upper bound, and their pointwise min is their greatest lower bound — both always exist within [latex]\mathcal F[/latex]. Pushing just does one comparison and one pointer copy ([latex]O(1)[/latex]); popping just removes the top record (its stored min-pointer disappears with it, automatically restoring the correct min for what's now on top) ([latex]O(1)[/latex]); MIN just reads the top record's stored pointer ([latex]O(1)[/latex]). This works and keeps everything [latex]O(1)[/latex]. A single global pointer to the current minimum fails on POP: if you pop exactly the minimum record, you have no way to find the next-smallest without scanning the rest of the stack. A sorted auxiliary array would need [latex]O(n)[/latex] shifting on push to keep it sorted. A min-heap would make push/pop cost [latex]O(\log n)[/latex] instead of [latex]O(1)[/latex], violating the "don't slow down the standard operations" requirement. Answer: Keep, with every record, a pointer to the record with the smallest key below it. Click here for detail solution

[latex]P = \{P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4\} [/latex] consists of all active processes in an operating system.  
[latex]R = \{R_1, R_2, R_3, R_4\} [/latex] consists of single instances of distinct types of resources in the system. The resource allocation graph has the following assignment and claim edges. [latex]
\text{Assignment edges: } R_1 \to P_1,  R_2 \to P_2,  R_3 \to P_3,  R_4 \to P_4 
[/latex] (the assignment edge [latex]R_1 \to P_1[/latex] means resource [latex]R_1[/latex] is assigned to process [latex]P_1[/latex], and so on for others) [latex]
\text{Claim edges: } P_1 \to R_2, P_2 \to R_3, P_3 \to R_1, P_2 \to R_4, P_4 \to R_2
[/latex] (the claim edge [latex]P_1 \to R_2[/latex] means process [latex]P_1[/latex] is waiting for resource [latex]R_2[/latex], and so on for others) Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT?

options.A: Aborting [latex]P_1 [/latex] makes the system deadlock free.
options.B: Aborting [latex]P_3 [/latex] makes the system deadlock free.
options.C: Aborting [latex]P_2 [/latex] makes the system deadlock free.
options.D: Aborting [latex]P_1 [/latex] and [latex]P_4 [/latex] makes the system deadlock free.

questions.explanation: Build the resource-allocation graph and look for cycles (with single-instance resources, a cycle means deadlock): Cycle A: [latex]P_1\to R_2\to P_2\to R_3\to P_3\to R_1\to P_1[/latex] (involving [latex]P_1,P_2,P_3[/latex]). Cycle B: [latex]P_2\to R_4\to P_4\to R_2\to P_2[/latex] (involving [latex]P_2,P_4[/latex]). Both cycles share [latex]P_2[/latex] as a common process. Aborting [latex]P_2[/latex] alone breaks both cycles simultaneously (removing [latex]P_2[/latex]'s edges collapses both cycles at once) — system becomes deadlock-free. Aborting [latex]P_1[/latex] alone only breaks Cycle A; Cycle B (which never involved [latex]P_1[/latex]) remains fully intact — still deadlocked. Similarly, aborting [latex]P_3[/latex] alone only touches Cycle A, leaving Cycle B untouched — still deadlocked. Aborting both [latex]P_1[/latex] and [latex]P_4[/latex] together: removing [latex]P_1[/latex] frees [latex]R_1[/latex] (letting [latex]P_3[/latex]'s wait resolve), and removing [latex]P_4[/latex] frees [latex]R_4[/latex] (letting [latex]P_2[/latex]'s wait for [latex]R_4[/latex] resolve); with both freed, the remaining chain ([latex]P_2,P_3[/latex]) can fully unwind — deadlock-free. Answer: Aborting P2 alone works; and aborting both P1 and P4 together works. Click here for detail solution

G1: S \to \text{if} E \text{ then } S \mid \text{if} E \text{ then } S \text{ else } S \mid a
[/latex] [latex]
E \to b
[/latex] [latex]
G2: S \to \text{if} E \text{ then } S \mid M
[/latex] [latex]
M \to \text{if} E \text{ then } M \text{ else } S \mid c
[/latex] [latex]
E \to b
[/latex] where [latex] if,then,else,a,b,c[/latex] are the terminals. Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?

In [latex]G2[/latex], despite the [latex]M[/latex]-split attempting to disambiguate dangling-else, [latex]S[/latex]'s own alternatives ([latex]S\to\text{if}\,E\,\text{then}\,S[/latex] and [latex]S\to M[/latex], where [latex]M[/latex] can itself start with "if") suffer the exact same kind of FIRST/FIRST conflict on seeing "if" — so [latex]G2[/latex] is not LL(1) either. (Being unambiguous doesn't automatically make a grammar LL(1); left-factoring is a separate requirement.) Ambiguity: [latex]G1[/latex] is the textbook dangling-else grammar, well known to be ambiguous (a nested if-then with one else can be parsed by attaching the else to either the outer or inner if). questions.question: Let [latex]\Sigma = \{a, b, c\} [/latex]. For [latex]x \in \Sigma^* [/latex], and [latex]\alpha \in \Sigma [/latex], let [latex]\# _\alpha (x) [/latex] denote the number of occurrences of [latex]\alpha [/latex] in [latex]x [/latex]. Which one or more of the following option(s) define(s) regular language(s)?

options.B: [latex]\{ a, b \}^* \cap \{ a^m b^n c^{m-n} \mid m \geq n \geq 0 \} [/latex]

questions.explanation: [latex]\{a^mb^n\mid m,n\ge0\}[/latex]: simply any number of [latex]a[/latex]'s followed by any number of [latex]b[/latex]'s, with no relationship required between the two counts — matched exactly by the regular expression [latex]a^*b^*[/latex]. Regular. [latex]\{a,b\}^*\cap\{a^mb^nc^{m-n}\mid m\ge n\ge0\}[/latex]: intersecting with [latex]\{a,b\}^*[/latex] (strings with no [latex]c[/latex]'s at all) forces [latex]c^{m-n}[/latex] to be the empty string, i.e. [latex]m=n[/latex] exactly. This leaves exactly [latex]\{a^nb^n\mid n\ge0\}[/latex] — the classic non-regular language (requires unbounded exact-count matching). Not regular. [latex]\{w\mid\#_a(w)\equiv2\pmod7,\ \#_b(w)\equiv3\pmod9\}[/latex]: despite unbounded counts of [latex]a[/latex]'s and [latex]b[/latex]'s, only their values modulo a fixed number matter, which needs only [latex]7\times9=63[/latex] distinct states to track (a finite automaton cycling through remainders). Regular. [latex]\{w\mid\#_a(w)\equiv2\pmod7,\ \#_a(w)=\#_b(w)\}[/latex]: the modular part alone would be fine, but the additional requirement of exact equality between [latex]\#_a(w)[/latex] and [latex]\#_b(w)[/latex] (unbounded, not just modular) needs unbounded memory. Not regular. Answer: {a^m b^n} and the mod-7/mod-9 language are both regular. Click here for detail solution

questions.question: A quadratic polynomial [latex](x - \alpha)(x - \beta)[/latex] over complex numbers is said to be square invariant if [latex](x - \alpha)(x - \beta) = (x - \alpha^2)(x - \beta^2)[/latex]. (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation: [latex](x-\alpha)(x-\beta)=(x-\alpha^2)(x-\beta^2)[/latex] for all [latex]x[/latex] means the root sets [latex]\{\alpha,\beta\}[/latex] and [latex]\{\alpha^2,\beta^2\}[/latex] must be identical (as unordered pairs). Two cases: Case 1 (each root is individually fixed by squaring): [latex]\alpha^2=\alpha,\ \beta^2=\beta[/latex], forcing each of [latex]\alpha,\beta[/latex] independently into [latex]\{0,1\}[/latex] (the only solutions of [latex]z^2=z[/latex]). Besides the [latex]\alpha=0,1[/latex] solutions already counted, this adds the genuinely new pair of primitive cube roots of unity [latex]\{\omega,\omega^2\}[/latex] (distinct, non-repeated roots). So there are [latex]4[/latex] distinct square-invariant polynomials total: [latex]\{0,0\},\{1,1\},\{0,1\},\{\omega,\omega^2\}[/latex], of which exactly [latex]2[/latex] ([latex]\{0,0\}[/latex] and [latex]\{1,1\}[/latex]) have equal (repeated) roots.
